claim: Anthropic took three distinct policy positions on subscription-vs-automation economics within three months: a February 20, 2026 legal-terms update prohibiting subscription OAuth tokens in third-party products (unenforced at first), April 4, 2026 active enforcement against OpenClaw specifically, and a May 13, 2026 announcement of a metered Agent SDK credit (effective June 15) that was then paused hours before taking effect.
stance_target: Anthropic's subscription-automation enforcement policy has been volatile and inconsistently rolled out across 2026, rather than a single stable rule
quoted_support: between April and June 2026, Anthropic banned third-party tools from Claude subscriptions, announced a repricing that would have billed them at full API rates, and then paused the whole plan hours before it took effect. Three positions in three months.

claim: Anthropic's April 4, 2026 enforcement action specifically targeted OpenClaw, estimated to have 135,000+ running instances at the time, requiring affected usage to move to pay-as-you-go billing or a separate API key; Claude Code lead Boris Cherny stated subscriptions 'weren't built for the usage patterns of these third-party tools.'
stance_target: Anthropic's enforcement against subscription automation targeted a specific high-volume third-party tool ecosystem with an identifiable instance count
quoted_support: Claude Pro and Max subscribers can no longer route their plan's usage through third-party harnesses, starting with OpenClaw, the open-source agent framework with an estimated 135,000+ instances running at the time... Claude Code lead Boris Cherny said subscriptions 'weren't built for the usage patterns of these third-party tools.'

claim: VentureBeat reported some OpenClaw users consuming hundreds or thousands of dollars of API-equivalent tokens per month on a $200 flat-rate Claude plan prior to enforcement -- an over 5x gap between flat-subscription pricing and equivalent metered API cost for heavy agentic use.
stance_target: flat-rate consumer subscriptions, prior to enforcement, substantially subsidized heavy agentic token consumption relative to metered API pricing
scope_conditions: OpenClaw + Claude $200 subscription, before April 2026 enforcement
quoted_support: VentureBeat reported some OpenClaw users consuming hundreds or thousands of dollars of tokens per month on a $200 plan. Analysts cited a gap of more than 5x between flat-subscription pricing and equivalent API cost for heavy agentic use.

claim: OpenAI positioned itself as the permissive competitor to Anthropic's crackdown: it hired OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger, shipped a $100 ChatGPT tier with 5x Codex limits in April 2026 aimed at users Anthropic had just restricted, and staff publicly called OpenAI's own terms 'quite permissive' toward OpenCode-style third-party projects.
stance_target: competitive dynamics where one vendor's automation crackdown drives migration to a rival vendor's subscription rather than metered billing
quoted_support: OpenAI is deliberately playing the open counterpart. Codex works with ChatGPT sign-in across third-party clients, OpenAI staff have publicly called their terms 'quite permissive' toward projects like OpenCode, and the company hired Steinberger... In April OpenAI shipped a $100 ChatGPT tier with 5x Codex limits, aimed squarely at the users Anthropic had just restricted.

claim: The widely cited '15-30x subsidy' figure for Claude subscriptions vs. API-equivalent agentic usage traces to a single source (fazm.ai, relayed via Zed's engineering blog) and should be treated with caution as an unverified single-source estimate, though the directional claim (subscriptions substantially subsidize heavy agent usage) is not disputed.
stance_target: reliability of the specific multiplier figure used across multiple secondary sources to characterize the subscription-API cost gap
scope_conditions: Claude subscription vs. API cost comparison, 2026
quoted_support: That figure comes from a single source (fazm.ai), so treat the exact multiple with caution, but the direction is not in dispute.
